items.rule: Fractions must have a common denominator before their numerators can be added or subtracted.
Multiply numerators together and denominators together. Cancel common factors before multiplying when convenient.
To divide by a fraction, multiply by its reciprocal.
Divide all parts of a ratio by their greatest common factor.
If two quantities vary directly, their ratio remains constant.
If one quantity increases while another decreases so that their product remains constant, they are inversely proportional.
items.example: 4\text{ workers take }12\text{ days}\implies6\text{ workers take }8\text{ days}

items.rule: Percent means 'per hundred'. Convert a fraction to a percent by multiplying by 100.
To find p% of a quantity N, multiply N by p/100.
Increase by p% means multiply the original quantity by 1+p/100.
Decrease by p% means multiply the original quantity by 1-p/100.
When a final value is given after a percentage change, divide by the appropriate multiplier to recover the original.
For positive fractions, cross-multiplication gives a reliable comparison without converting to decimals.
Numbers farther to the right on the number line are greater.

concepts.title: 1. Fraction Arithmetic
concepts.subtitle: Operate, Simplify, and Control Denominators
concepts.summary: Fractions require different strategies for addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division. Addition and subtraction need a common denominator, while multiplication and division can often be simplified before calculating.

points.text: Add/Subtract: Find a common denominator first, then combine numerators.
Multiply: Multiply numerators and denominators, cancelling common factors early when possible.
Divide: Multiply by the reciprocal of the second fraction.
Mixed Numbers: Convert mixed numbers to improper fractions before performing the operation unless a direct decomposition is clearly simpler.

concepts.trap: Never add or subtract denominators directly. Denominators describe the unit size and must first be made common.

concepts.title: 2. Ratio & Proportion
concepts.subtitle: Scale, Compare, and Use the Unitary Method
concepts.summary: A ratio compares quantities of the same kind, while a proportion states that two ratios are equal. Direct proportion keeps a constant ratio; inverse proportion keeps a constant product.

points.text: Simplest Ratio: Divide every term by the HCF of the ratio terms.
Unitary Method: Find the value for one unit first, then scale to the required number of units.
Direct Proportion: Same multiplier means both quantities move in the same direction.
Inverse Proportion: As one quantity is multiplied by a factor, the other is divided by that factor.

concepts.trap: Before setting up a proportion, check that corresponding quantities are paired in the same order and units.

concepts.title: 3. Percentage Conversions
concepts.subtitle: Move Between Fraction, Decimal, and Percent
concepts.summary: Fractions, decimals, and percentages are different representations of the same quantity. Percentage change problems become easier when translated into multipliers.

points.text: Reverse Percent: Undo the multiplier rather than subtracting the percentage from the final value.

concepts.trap: A 20% increase followed by a 20% decrease does not return exactly to the original value because the second 20% is calculated from a different base.

concepts.title: 4. Comparison and Ordering
concepts.subtitle: Put Different Representations on One Number Line
concepts.summary: To compare fractions, decimals, and percentages, convert them into a common representation or use exact cross-multiplication. Then order them from smallest to largest or vice versa.

points.text: Decimals and Percentages: Convert percentages to decimals by dividing by 100.
Common Benchmark: Compare quantities to familiar values such as 0, 1/2, 1, or 100%.
Number Line: Greater values are always farther to the right.

concepts.trap: Do not compare numerator with numerator and denominator with denominator independently. The whole fraction determines the value.

option_details.explanation: A decimal becomes a percentage by multiplying by 100 and attaching the percent symbol.
Dividing by 100 would make the value smaller.
The conversion factor is 100%, not 10%.
Percentage conversion is multiplicative, not additive.

steps.rubric_text: Did you multiply the decimal by 100?
steps.hint: Move the decimal point two places right.
